analysis.one_liner: Requires a five-business-day waiting period and police background check before handgun sales.
analysis.headline: Introduced by the Senate Majority Leader in the final weeks of 1992, the bill was placed on the Senate calendar but never came up for a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it unlawful for licensed gun dealers to hand over a handgun until five business days had passed and the buyer's local police chief had checked for a criminal record or other legal bar. It would keep this waiting-period system in place until the Attorney General certified that a national instant background check system was running, then require dealers to check that system before every sale instead. It would also bar use of the system to build a gun registry and send federal grants to states to computerize criminal records.
analysis.who_benefits: People in communities affected by handgun violence: the waiting period and local police check are designed to stop sales to convicted felons, fugitives, drug users, and others legally barred from owning guns. Lawful buyers who value a cooling-off period also benefit, and local police departments gain federal grant money to modernize criminal records.

how_it_helps.text: Requires licensed dealers to wait five business days after notifying the buyer's chief law enforcement officer, giving police time to check state, local, and national records for a criminal history or other legal impediment before the sale goes through.

Requires buyers to sign a statement that they are not under indictment, not convicted of a crime punishable by more than a year, not a fugitive, not an unlawful drug user, not adjudicated mentally defective, not illegally in the country, not dishonorably discharged, and have not renounced citizenship.
Dealers who knowingly skip the check can face license suspension or revocation and fines up to $5,000, and knowing violations carry fines up to $1,000 and up to a year in prison.
Authorizes $100 million in grants to help states computerize criminal history records and connect them to the national system, with priority to states with the worst records.
Explicitly bars federal use of the system to create a registration system for firearms, owners, or transactions, except for people already barred from owning guns.

analysis.who_pays: Licensed gun dealers, importers, and manufacturers, who must run the checks, keep compliance records, and face fines and license action for violations; buyers face a delay of at least five business days; local police chiefs absorb the work of running checks on every handgun purchase.

drawbacks.text: Every lawful handgun purchase is delayed at least five business days, and buyers in remote areas or urgent situations bear that delay even if they have clean records; the bill includes an exception for people who document an immediate threat to their life or household.

Local chief law enforcement officers must make a reasonable effort to complete a records check within five business days for every proposed sale, a workload the bill shifts onto local police without dedicated operating funding; the $100 million grant authorization is subject to appropriations.

The criminal penalty for violations is modest — up to $1,000 and one year — and officials are shielded from damage lawsuits whether they fail to stop an unlawful sale or stop a lawful one, which limits accountability on both sides.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The burden is real but narrow: a short delay for buyers and paperwork for dealers and police chiefs, weighed against keeping handguns from people legally barred from having them. The bill is built as a compromise — it requires police checks only until a national instant system exists, destroys check records after twenty business days, bans building a registry from the data, and exempts states with valid permits or their own verification systems. The main design weakness is that it leans on local police who get grants only if Congress appropriates the money.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced by the Senate Majority Leader in the last weeks of the 102nd Congress, it was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar but was never brought to the floor for a vote before that Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: George J. Mitchell (D-ME), the Senate Majority Leader, introduced the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act on September 28, 1992, with no cosponsors listed.
The Senate read the bill twice — on September 28 and September 29, 1992 — and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 749.
No further action appears in the record: no committee referral, no floor debate, no roll-call vote, before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of the waiting period — chiefly gun dealers and the gun-rights lobby — avoided the requirement for the life of that Congress, though a successor Brady bill became law the following year.

for.name: George J. Mitchell
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill in the Senate in the closing weeks of the 102nd Congress and had it placed on the legislative calendar.

against.name: Senate leadership that never scheduled floor action
against.what_they_did: Left the bill on the Senate calendar under General Orders without bringing it to the floor for debate or a vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the Brady waiting-period bill and pressed senators to keep it from reaching a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no cosponsors are on record, so the roll-call record shows only that the Democratic Majority Leader sponsored it and the Senate never acted on it.

industries.note: Dealers would have to hold each handgun sale for five business days, notify local police, keep compliance records, and face license suspension, revocation, or fines up to $5,000 for knowingly skipping the check. Their interest in selling without delay runs against the waiting period's purpose of screening out prohibited buyers.

The bill applies the same check-and-wait requirements to licensed manufacturers and importers selling to individuals, adding compliance costs and potentially blocking some sales that would otherwise go through.

Police chiefs gain the duty to run records checks on every proposed handgun sale — an added workload — but the bill also authorizes $100 million in federal grants to computerize and connect state criminal records, which improves their own record systems.
